content:
Let \(r_x\) be the number of papers containing \(x\).

For any number \(x\), take a paper \(B\) not containing \(x\). Such a paper must exist; otherwise all papers contain \(x\), and the \(2n\) other entries would all have to be distinct, requiring \(2n+1\le n\), impossible.

Paper \(B\) has 3 numbers and must intersect each of the \(r_x\) papers containing \(x\). No two of those papers can intersect \(B\) in the same number, because then they would share both \(x\) and that number. Hence
\[
r_x\le 3.
\]

Total number of occurrences is
\[
\sum_{x=1}^n r_x = 3n.
\]
Since each \(r_x\le 3\), equality forces
\[
r_x=3 \quad \text{for every } x=1,\dots,n.
\]

Now fix a number \(x\). The 3 papers containing \(x\) have all their other 6 numbers distinct. Any paper not containing \(x\) must intersect each of those 3 papers, so it contains exactly one number from each of their two remaining numbers.

There are \(n-3\) papers not containing \(x\), giving \(3(n-3)\) occurrences among those papers. But each of the 6 other numbers appears exactly \(3-1=2\) times outside the papers containing \(x\), giving \(6\cdot 2=12\) occurrences. Thus
\[
3(n-3)=12 \implies n=7.
\]

Therefore the sum of all written numbers is
\[
3(1+2+\cdots+7)=3\cdot 28=84.
\]

\[
\boxed{84}
\]
